analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved opening the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing on a 29-13 vote, but the bill never received a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the long-standing ban on drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and order the Interior Department to run lease sales on the refuge's coastal plain. It would treat a 1987 environmental review as good enough for the pre-leasing steps, narrow the scope of any new environmental study, and push legal challenges into a single court on a short clock with no taxpayer-paid attorney fees. Half of the money from the leases would go to the Treasury, and the bill includes wildlife protections, Native hiring goals, and a ban on exporting the oil.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to a large new drilling frontier that has been off-limits since 1980, with a faster permitting path, narrower environmental review, and shorter, harder-to-win court challenges. Alaska Native corporations would receive long-promised land title conveyances. The Treasury would collect half of the bonus, rental, and royalty payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers and lease bidders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the section of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act that prohibits producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, and directs the Interior Department to run a competitive leasing program on the coastal plain.

It orders the Secretary to offer at least 50,000 acres for lease within 22 months of enactment, with additional 50,000-acre offerings at 6-, 12-, and 18-month intervals, and to issue leases within 90 days of each sale.
Leases must pay a royalty of at least 12.5 percent, and half of all bonus, rental, and royalty revenue from the program must be deposited in the Treasury.

The bill requires seasonal closings to protect caribou calving areas, full lessee liability for reclamation, use of the best commercially available drilling technology, and a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for fish, wildlife, subsistence resources, and the environment.

Leases must prohibit export of the oil produced, require best efforts to provide a fair share of employment and contracting for Alaska Natives and Alaska Native corporations, and require lessees to negotiate labor agreements covering laborers and mechanics on production, maintenance, and construction.
The bill's stated purpose is to secure energy supplies for the Pacific Coast of the United States, lower prices, and reduce imports.

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the permanent opening of a wildlife refuge to industrial development, with environmental review of the leasing program based largely on a 1987 study and a new study that would not even consider the option of not leasing. Public comment would be limited to 20 days and only comments addressing the Interior Department's preferred action. Anyone suing over the program would have to go to one court, the D.C. Circuit, within tight deadlines, and would face a presumption that the Department's analysis is correct. Subsistence users of the coastal plain would face the risk to wildlife and habitat that the bill's protections attempt but do not guarantee to prevent.

drawbacks.text: The bill deems the 1987 Final Legislative Environmental Impact Statement sufficient to satisfy modern environmental review law for pre-leasing steps, and bars the Secretary from analyzing a non-leasing alternative in the new environmental impact statement, considering only a preferred action and a single leasing alternative.

The Secretary would only be required to consider public comments filed within 20 days that specifically address the preferred action, and compliance with the bill would be deemed to satisfy all environmental review requirements for leasing.

Judicial challenges would be limited to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, most complaints would face a 90-day deadline, the Secretary's preferred course of action and environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless shown otherwise by clear and convincing evidence, and challengers could not recover attorney fees or court costs from the government.
The Secretary's sole authority to close any part of the coastal plain to drilling would be the authority written into this bill, removing other existing grounds for keeping lands off-limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would create a new domestic oil frontier with royalties, Native hiring goals, wildlife stipulations, and an export ban, but those safeguards sit alongside a sharply shortened environmental review, a 20-day comment window, and a single-court challenge path that would make the program very difficult to stop or fix later. The environmental gains to the public from cheaper energy would be small and delayed, since even under the bill's own schedule the first tracts would not be offered for lease until at least 22 months after enactment, while the loss of refuge protections would be permanent. A design that paired new drilling with genuine, current environmental review would have been a fairer trade than what this bill offered.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved it 29-13 and put it on the Union Calendar, which is the list of bills awaiting floor action, but no House vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Doc Hastings of Washington, chair of the House Natural Resources Committee, introduced the bill on November 14, 2011, together with Representative Don Young of Alaska.
On February 1, 2012, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 29 to 13, and it was formally reported on February 9, 2012.
The reported bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 273, meaning it was ready and waiting for a vote by the full House.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died without the House ever deciding it.
The bill's cosponsors were three Republicans, and no floor vote or Senate action on the bill appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died before a floor vote, the drilling ban on the Arctic Refuge coastal plain stayed in place, so conservation, wildlife, and subsistence interests came out ahead. Oil and gas companies lost the access the bill would have handed them, though they lost it through inaction rather than an affirmative rejection, so the question never got a direct answer from the full Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Conservation interests; drillers never got a vote

for.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his committee, which reported it as amended on a 29-13 vote.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Joined Hastings in introducing the bill to open the Alaska refuge coastal plain to drilling.

for.name: House Natural Resources Committee majority
for.role: Committee members voting to report the bill
for.what_they_did: Voted 29-13 to order the bill reported as amended on February 1, 2012.

against.name: 13 House Natural Resources Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting no in markup
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported when the committee considered it on February 1, 2012.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote by the full House before the Congress ended, leaving it on the Union Calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor in the record was a Republican, and the committee approved it 29-13, though the record does not break down the parties on that vote; no full-chamber vote ever took place to show where the whole House stood.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production companies
industries.note: The bill hands drillers access to the Arctic Refuge coastal plain, a frontier closed to them since 1980, while cutting the environmental review, public comment, and court access that would otherwise slow or block them. The public keeps only half the revenue from leases on federal land, and bears the permanent loss of refuge protections.

The bill directs the Secretary to issue rights-of-way and easements across the coastal plain for moving the oil and gas produced there, which would expand pipeline and transport work tied to the new leases.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys long-owed land titles to these corporations, settling entitlements under earlier agreements. Arctic Slope Regional Corporation also stands to benefit from subsurface and development interests in the region.

industries.industry: Refuge recreation, hunting, and subsistence interests
industries.note: Opening the coastal plain to drilling, roads, and facilities puts at risk the wildlife, habitat, and subsistence hunting and fishing that these groups and ordinary Alaskans rely on, a cost the bill's seasonal limits and stipulations attempt but cannot guarantee to prevent.
